name: Katu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wallace, Judith M. 1969. Katu phonemes. Mon-Khmer Studies 3: 64-73. (Primary phonological description; Low Katu of Anđiềm, Quảng Nam, Vietnam, with reference to Phúhòa Low Katu and Chuah High Katu.) Corroborated by Costello, Nancy A. 1991. Nooq Paraaq Katu / Katu Dictionary: Katu-Vietnamese-English (Tủ Sách Ngôn-Ngữ Dân-Tộc Thiểu-Số Việt-Nam, cuốn 5, phần 2). Manila: Summer Institute of Linguistics. Front matter, 'Orthography' > 'Word Structure and Phoneme Distribution' (secondary).
catalog_locator: Wallace 1969, sec. 3 'Word Structure and phoneme Distribution', p. 69 (stress statement); p. 71 (presyllable vowels v2, v3 'usually actualize as an unstressed [ə]'; four-syllable maximum, examples tapasaruum, tapaglâk); p. 64 (identity paragraph). Secondary: Costello 1991, front matter 'Orthography' > 'Word Structure and Phoneme Distribution' (p. 1 of the Rosetta Project excerpt).
catalog_quote: The katu word has a main syllable which can be precedeŋ by one, two, or three presyllables. The word can be symbolized as c₃v/c₂v/c₁v/ MS. (Lower case is used for presyllable symbols, upper case for main syllable symbols.) The main syllable always receives the major stress. c₃v and c₂v are always affixes, and c₁v sometimes is. The vowel position in all presyllables is filled by /a/. In a c₁v syllable, /a/ tends to actualize as [i] after alveopalatals, [ə] after /b,d,n,ŋ/ [ʌ] after /q,g,k,l,m,p,t/, and [a[ after /h,r/. In some sub-dialects /a/ actualizes as vocalic [r] in v₁ position. ... v₂ and v₃ usually actualize as an unstressed [ə]. ... No consonant clusters have been found in four-syllable words. ... Examples of maximum word expansion: tapasaruum « cause each other to fall », tapaglâk « cause each other to carry ».
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The Katu word has a main syllable which can be preceded by one, two or three presyllables. The word can be symbolised as CV3/CV2/CV1/MS. CV3 and CV2 are always affixes, whereas CV1 is rarely an affix. Presyllables are always unstressed. The main syllable MS can be symbolised as CV±C or CCV.

The section "Word Structure and Phoneme Distribution" reads, verbatim: "The Katu word has a main syllable which can be preceded by one, two or three presyllables. This matches the reported quote exactly (the PDF's own text omits this paragraph; the djvu scanned has it with minor scanned garbling, and the page scan settles it). The page…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Katu words are sesquisyllabic: a full main syllable (CV(C) or CCV) optionally preceded by up to three reduced presyllables (mostly affixes). Presyllables are never stressed, so stress falls on the main syllable, which is always the last syllable of the word (i.e. word-final stress in every polysyllable; monosyllables are the main syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the statement is absolute ('always unstressed').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (dictionary headwords/citation forms); the dictionary covers Low Katu of An-Diem (default, unmarked) and Phu-Hoa, plus High Katu (hk), all in Quang Nam, Vietnam. The statement is a one-line word-structure note in a dictionary's orthography preface, not a full phonological analysis; the dedicated phonology paper (Wallace 1969, 'Katu phonemes') could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Costello 1991 dictionary) describes the Vietnam Katu of Quang Nam province: Low Katu of An-Diem (default) and Phu-Hoa, plus High Katu; all fall under Glottolog east1236 (Eastern Katu, ktv; alternate names include High Katu, Kantu, Phuong). Costello & Sulavan 1996 states the Lao PDR dialect differs only in a few predictable phonetic details (presyllable inventory reduced to one presyllable). Western Katu (west2398, kuf) is a separate Glottolog language and is not what these sources describe.

tone_statements.citation: Nguyễn Đăng Châu. n.d. [c. 2005-2008]. Ngữ âm tiếng Cơ Tu và vấn đề chữ viết tiếng Cơ Tu [Cơ Tu phonetics and the question of a Cơ Tu script] (running head: 'Cơ cấu ngữ âm tiếng Cơ Tu'). Khoa Ngữ văn, Đại học Sư phạm Đà Nẵng. Unpublished monograph / research report (Mở đầu; Ch. 1 Ngữ âm tiếng Cơ Tu; Ch. 2 Ngữ âm Cơ Tu ở các địa phương; Ch. 3 Chữ viết tiếng Cơ Tu; Kết luận; Cơ Tu-Việt-English wordlist; 44 references), full text posted on the blog 'Dạy học tiếng Việt'.
tone_statements.quote: Là một ngôn ngữ chưa hình thành thanh điệu, hệ thống phụ âm tiếng Cơ Tu chắc chắn mang trong mình nó những đặc trưng cổ xưa mà những ngôn ngữ anh em trong gia đình Môn – Khmer thanh điệu hóa từng có. [...] (§1.4.2:) Do đó, có thể nói rằng tuy các âm vị cuối /-h/ và /-[ʔ]/ là giải pháp hợp lí hiện nay vì cái gọi là hiện tượng thanh điệu chưa rõ rệt. Nhưng có thể trong tương lai, chúng dần dần chỉ còn là thuộc tính của hiện tượng ngôn điệu nếu như ngôn ngữ này tiếp tục tồn tại và phát triển.
tone_statements.translation: Being a language that has not yet formed tones, the Cơ Tu consonant system certainly retains within it the archaic features that its tonalised sister languages in the Mon-Khmer family once had. [...] Hence one may say that the final phonemes /-h/ and /-ʔ/ are the reasonable solution at present, because the so-called tone phenomenon is not yet clear-cut. But possibly, in the future, they will gradually become mere attributes of a prosodic (tonal) phenomenon, if this language continues to exist and develop.

sources.citation: Gehrmann, Ryan & Johanna Conver. 2015. Katuic phonological features. Mon-Khmer Studies 44 (Notes, Reviews, Data-Papers): lv-lxvii. ISSN 0147-5207.
sources.note: §4 'Register Systems' places the Katu languages alone among Katuic at the 'conservative' stage of the Khmer registrogenesis model — Proto-Katuic voiced stops retained, no breathy/modal register split — whereas all other Katuic groups (West Katuic, Kriang, Ta'oi, Pacoh) have transitional-to-restructured register systems; i.e. Katu has neither register nor tone. No stress statement.

tone.quote: The first ‘conservative’ stage applies to a language with voiced and voiceless initial stops. [...] Within Katuic, only the Katu languages have retained the PK voiced stop series and remained at the conservative stage. All other Katuic languages are in the transitional to restructuring stages, like West Katuic and Kriang languages, though the Pacoh and Ta’oi register systems have departed from the Khmer model trajectory and developed in novel ways.
